prompt:
You are a careful equity research analyst. Assess the competitive advantages (economic moat) and pricing power of the publicly listed company "ServiceNow, Inc." (ticker NOW), and list its competitors. Use the most recent information you know. Never invent figures: use null when unsure. Be specific (products, numbers, years).

Reply with ONLY one JSON object, no other text, in exactly this shape:
{
 "name": "official company name", "ticker": "NOW", "industry": "industry in a few words",
 "markets": ["the main product markets it competes in"],
 "mission": {"statement": "the company's own official mission statement, word for word as it publishes it; null if you are not sure of the exact wording (never paraphrase here)",
             "source": "where it is published, e.g. company website or 2025 annual report, or null",
             "plain": "what the mission means, in one short simple sentence"},
 "about": {"plain": "3-4 short sentences explaining what the company does, in simple everyday words a 12-year-old would understand; no jargon",
           "customers": "who buys from it, in one simple sentence",
           "everyday": "one sentence linking it to something ordinary people know or use, or null",
           "money": [ {"part": "business line in simple words", "share": decimal share of sales or null, "plain": "what it sells there, in a few simple words", "tag": "main|new|moonshot"} ]  (its main ways of making money, largest first, up to 6; also include any new business line or one with explosive, moonshot potential even if its sales are still small. tag: "main" = an established line that brings in a large part of sales; "new" = launched or entered in roughly the last 3 years; "moonshot" = could grow many times over or reshape the company, e.g. a new technology or market, even if unproven. Give each line one tag, the one that fits best)},
 "summary": "2-3 plain-English sentences on whether and why it has a competitive advantage",
 "pricingPower": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "specific evidence, e.g. price rises and what happened to volumes"},
 "moats": [ {"source": one of ["Brand and intangible assets","Switching costs","Network effects","Cost advantage and scale","Efficient scale","Counter-positioning","Process power (hard-to-copy know-how)","Cornered resource (exclusive asset or talent)"], "strength": "strong|moderate|weak|none", "evidence": "one or two specific sentences"} ]  (all 8 sources, in that order),
 "customers": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "customer satisfaction and loyalty: retention, NPS, reviews, repeat purchase"},
 "talent": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "ability to attract and keep top talent: employer rankings, reputation, pay"},
 "product": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "is the product best in class? independent benchmarks, awards, ecosystem"},
 "competitors": [ {"name": "company name", "ticker": "main listing ticker (exchange suffix if not US, e.g. 005930.KS) or null if private",
                   "usTicker": "ticker of its US listing or ADR that files reports with the SEC, or null", "overlap": "high|medium|low",
                   "note": "where they compete"} ]  (every significant competitor, most direct first, up to 15; include major private ones with ticker null),
 "estimates": [ {"name": "company name", "fy": "FY2025", "currency": "USD", "revenueUSDm": number, "revenueGrowth3y": decimal, "grossMargin": decimal, "operatingMargin": decimal, "netMargin": decimal} ]
   (approximate latest fiscal-year figures for the company itself and for every listed competitor; decimals, e.g. 0.42; null if unknown),
 "marketShare": [ {"market": "market name", "measure": "revenue|units|shipments|...", "latestYear": "2025", "earlierYear": "2020",
                   "rows": [ {"name": "company name", "latest": decimal or null, "earlier": decimal or null} ] } ]  (up to 3 of its main markets, the company and its main rivals),
 "threats": ["specific things that could weaken its advantage"],
 "ceo": {"name": "current CEO", "founder": true or false, "since": "YYYY", "background": "e.g. electrical engineer, Stanford MBA"},
 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence with names, numbers or examples"} }  for EVERY id below:
   "c1": Rule Breaker #1: is it the leader of an important industry that is still emerging and growing fast?
   "c2": Rule Breaker #2: why do customers choose it over rivals (brand, better value, innovation, culture, leadership), and is that advantage hard to copy and likely to last many years?
   "c3": Rule Breaker #5: do ordinary people recognise the name, is it the default leader in its field (like Google, Amazon, NVIDIA, Tesla, Intuitive Surgical, Netflix), and would customers recommend its product?
   "c4": Does it have an inspiring mission it keeps emphasising, with management driven by purpose rather than money? If it spends 10 years doing this, would it matter?
   "c6": What is the general public consensus about the company and its products or services? When people hear the name, what are the first few descriptive words that come to mind? Start the evidence with those words in quotes (e.g. “innovative, premium, reliable”), then say whether that impression is mostly positive.
   "c7": Is its total addressable market large and growing, riding a secular trend (like CRWD, NVDA, TSLA, AMZN)?
   "c8": Does it have room to expand into big new markets: in its name, its technology or its vision?
   "m1": Is the CEO a visionary with a clear picture of the future?
   "m2": Is the CEO a founder (or acting like one): long-term thinking, working extraordinarily hard, pouring heart and soul into building something that outlives them?
   "m4": Does the CEO lead by serving employees and customers?
   "m5": Has the CEO deliberately built a strong, distinctive culture that keeps inventing new products and technologies?
   "m6": Is the CEO deeply hands-on with the product and technology, ideally with an engineering background?
   "m7": Is the CEO a person of great character who cares about something bigger than profit? For successor CEOs: is stewardship aimed at the benefit of humanity?
   "m7b": Has the CEO been invited to give a commencement speech at a top university (Stanford, Harvard, MIT, etc.)? Name it.
   "m8b": Does the CEO have a distinctive, memorable personality (like Elon Musk, Alex Karp, Larry Page)?
   "m9": Has the CEO a strong record of execution and results?
   "m10": Is the CEO and company known for frugality (like Bezos's door desk)?
   "c10": Do its products solve problems for people all over the world, greatly improving the lives of a very large number of people (like NFLX, GOOG, ISRG)?
   "p2": Is what it builds extremely hard to do, and important to the world?
   "f1": Has revenue grown in almost every one of the last five years?
   "f2": Have gross and operating margins risen over the last five years?
   "f3": Is debt low compared with cash and cash flow, with positive shareholders' equity?
   "f4": Have operating income and operating cash flow risen over the last five years?
   "v1": Is its main product clearly the best in its field, with a practical reason an ordinary person can understand for choosing it over every alternative (like NVIDIA over AMD)?
   "v2": Is it widely seen as one of the best companies to work for (culture, mission, reputation, employer rankings)? Cite rankings.
   "c5": Do its products make the world better? If it disappeared overnight, who would notice and miss it, and why?
 "asOf": "YYYY-MM of the newest information you used"
}

result.name: ServiceNow, Inc.
result.industry: Enterprise cloud software (workflow automation and AI agents)
markets: IT service and IT operations management (ITSM, ITOM)
Employee workflows (HR service delivery, workplace services)
Low-code app development (App Engine, Creator workflows)
Security operations, IT risk and cyber exposure management (incl. Armis, Veza)
Enterprise AI agents and AI governance (Now Assist, AI Agents, AI Control Tower)

mission.statement: make the world work better for everyone
mission.plain: ServiceNow wants work at companies to run more smoothly for everyone involved.

about.plain: ServiceNow makes online software that big organisations use to get work done. When an employee's laptop breaks, a new worker needs a desk, or a customer has a problem, ServiceNow tracks the request and sends it to the right person or computer to fix it. It now adds AI helpers that can do many of these steps on their own. Companies pay a yearly subscription to use it.
about.customers: Large companies and governments, including about 90% of the Fortune 500, pay for yearly subscriptions.
about.everyday: When you file an IT help-desk ticket or HR request at a big employer and get updates by email, there is a good chance ServiceNow is running it behind the scenes.

money.plain: yearly access to its cloud platform for IT, HR, customer service and app building
help setting up and training on the software
AI add-ons that answer questions and finish tasks on their own; crossed $1 billion in annual contract value in 2026
finding and protecting every connected device and controlling who can access what
one place to run and govern all of a company's AI agents, plus sales and customer software

result.summary: ServiceNow has a wide competitive advantage built on deep switching costs: its single platform becomes the system of record for IT, HR and customer-service processes, and customers renewed at a 98% rate in Q4 2025. It holds an estimated 44.4% of the IT service management software market (Apps Run The World, 2024), far ahead of rivals. The main open question is whether AI agents from model makers and hyperscalers erode seat-based software, which drove a sharp 2026 share-price fall even as revenue grew 24% in Q2 2026.

pricingPower.evidence: ServiceNow sells premium Pro Plus and AI tiers at higher prices and customers keep expanding: renewal rate was 98% in Q4 2025, customers paying over $5M in annual contract value rose to 658 in Q2 2026 (up about 23%), and subscription revenue grew 24.5% that quarter; non-GAAP subscription gross margin is guided at 81% for 2026. It is moving to a hybrid seat-plus-consumption model (assist packs) for AI, which is still being proven.

moats.evidence: ServiceNow is the default name for IT service management among CIOs and is used by about 90% of the Fortune 500, but it is little known to consumers.

Customers build years of custom workflows, data (the CMDB) and integrations on the Now Platform; the renewal rate was 98% in Q4 2025 and remaining performance obligations reached $29.0 billion in Q2 2026.
An ecosystem of partners (Accenture, Deloitte, others), certified developers and a store of third-party apps adds value, but one customer's use does not directly make the product better for another.
With $13.3 billion of 2025 revenue and $3.0 billion of R&D spend, it can outspend specialist rivals like BMC Helix and Ivanti while keeping about 78% gross margins.
Enterprise software markets are large and open to many entrants; there is no natural limit on the number of competitors.
Its single-codebase, single-data-model platform was a counter to legacy on-premises IT tools, but AI-native agent start-ups and model makers now try to counter-position against seat-based software.
Two decades of workflow know-how and a single architecture let it release two major platform versions a year and add AI agents across every product.
It has no exclusive asset; its large installed base of process data on customers' systems is its closest equivalent.

customers.evidence: Renewal rate of 98% in Q4 2025; 658 customers with over $5M annual contract value in Q2 2026, up about 23%; about 8,700 customers at end of 2025 including about 90% of the Fortune 500.

talent.evidence: ServiceNow lists itself on the Fortune 100 Best Companies to Work For and Glassdoor Best Places to Work in Tech and AI 2026, with about 30,000 employees at June 30, 2026, and pays heavily in stock ($1.96 billion of stock compensation in 2025).

product.evidence: It holds an estimated 44.4% share of ITSM software (Apps Run The World, 2024), was named to Fast Company's Most Innovative Companies 2026 (Applied AI), and its Now Assist AI products crossed $1 billion in annual contract value in 2026.

competitors.name: Microsoft
competitors.note: Copilot and agent tools, Dynamics 365 customer service, Power Platform low-code and Intune endpoint management

competitors.note: Customer service/CRM, Agentforce AI agents and Slack-based IT service; competes as ServiceNow pushes into CRM

competitors.name: BMC Helix
competitors.note: Legacy ITSM and IT operations software (private, owned by KKR)

competitors.note: HR service delivery and employee workflows, and AI agents for HR

competitors.note: Business process and employee workflows, Joule AI agents

competitors.note: Enterprise applications and service management bundled with its ERP and HCM

competitors.name: Freshworks
competitors.note: Freshservice ITSM and Freshdesk customer service for mid-market firms

competitors.name: Pegasystems
competitors.note: Workflow automation and customer service for large enterprises

competitors.name: Palo Alto Networks
competitors.note: Security operations and exposure management, where Armis now competes

competitors.name: CrowdStrike
competitors.note: Security operations, asset and exposure management

competitors.name: OpenAI
competitors.note: Enterprise AI agents (e.g., agent platforms) that could take over work done in workflow software (private)

marketShare.market: Worldwide IT service management software (Apps Run The World)

threats: AI agents from model makers (OpenAI, Anthropic) and hyperscalers (Microsoft Copilot) could automate work without a workflow platform, cutting seat-based demand; this fear drove the 2026 software selloff.
A shift from per-seat to consumption pricing for AI could make revenue less predictable and pressure margins.
Integration risk and dilution of focus from large 2025-2026 acquisitions (Moveworks, Armis for $7.75 billion, Veza), which lifted goodwill to $9.8 billion and debt to $7.5 billion by June 2026.
GAAP margins are falling: Q2 2026 GAAP operating income was $162 million versus $358 million a year earlier, and GAAP gross margin fell to 70.5%.
Microsoft, Salesforce and Atlassian bundling cheaper service-desk and agent tools into products customers already own.
Security incidents on the platform (a June 2026 incident weighed on shares) could damage trust as a system of record.
Dependence on CEO Bill McDermott (born 1961) and key executives for the AI strategy.

ceo.name: Bill McDermott
ceo.background: Former SAP CEO (2010-2019) and Xerox sales executive; Dowling College bachelor's degree, Northwestern Kellogg MBA; also ServiceNow chairman

c1.evidence: ServiceNow leads IT service management with an estimated 44.4% share (Apps Run The World, 2024) and is positioning as the 'AI Control Tower' for enterprise AI agents, a young, fast-growing market; subscription revenue grew 24.5% in Q2 2026.

c2.evidence: Customers choose its single platform and data model that ties IT, HR and customer workflows together, and stay: renewal rate was 98% in Q4 2025 and RPO reached $29.0 billion, an advantage hard to copy after 20 years of building.

c3.evidence: It is the default choice for CIOs (about 90% of the Fortune 500 use it), but ordinary consumers rarely know the name.

c4.evidence: Its purpose 'make the world work better for everyone' is repeated in filings and on its website, but management messaging centres on financial targets such as $30 billion of subscription revenue by 2030 and the 'Rule of 56'.

c6.evidence: “enterprise, IT help desk, expensive, AI”: among business buyers the impression is mostly positive (reliable, powerful, market leader), though users often call it complex and costly, and most of the public has no impression at all.

c7.evidence: It rides enterprise AI and digital transformation; management targets $30 billion of subscription revenue by 2030 (May 2026 investor day), implying about 19% annual growth from 2026.

c8.evidence: Since 2019 it has expanded from IT into HR, customer service/CRM, low-code, security (Armis, Veza) and AI agent governance, and the 'Now' platform name is not tied to one market.

m1.evidence: McDermott has set a clear vision of ServiceNow as the 'defining AI enterprise software company of the 21st century' and the AI Control Tower that governs all of a company's agents.

m2.evidence: He is not the founder (Fred Luddy founded it in 2004), but he acts with an owner's intensity, buying about $3.0 million of stock in the open market on February 27, 2026 at about $104.60.

m4.evidence: McDermott emphasises customer success and employee culture, and ServiceNow appears on Fortune's 100 Best Companies to Work For, but there is limited independent evidence of servant leadership specifically.

m5.evidence: Under McDermott it built Now Assist and AI agents into every product and crossed $1 billion in AI annual contract value in 2026, while keeping a recognised workplace culture.

m6.evidence: McDermott is a sales and management executive (Xerox, SAP), not an engineer; product is led by others.

m7.evidence: He is known for resilience (he lost an eye in a 2015 accident and returned to lead SAP) and talks of purpose, but there is no clear evidence of stewardship aimed beyond the business.

m7b.evidence: No commencement speech by McDermott at Stanford, Harvard, MIT or a similar top university was found.

m8b.evidence: McDermott is known for a high-energy, salesman's style and memoir 'Winners Dream' (2014), a distinctive public persona though less famous than Musk or Karp.

m9.evidence: Since he became CEO in 2019, revenue rose from $4.5 billion (2020) to $13.3 billion (2025) and GAAP operating income from $199 million to $1.82 billion.

m10.evidence: ServiceNow is not known for frugality; it pays about $2 billion a year in stock compensation and spent about $10 billion on acquisitions in 2025-2026.

c10.evidence: Its software quietly speeds up IT, HR and customer service for millions of employees at about 8,700 organisations worldwide, but it improves work processes rather than transforming people's lives.

p2.evidence: Building a single reliable platform that runs mission-critical processes for most of the Fortune 500 is hard, but it is business software rather than a breakthrough technology.

f1.evidence: Revenue grew every year: $4.52 billion (2020), $5.90B, $7.25B, $8.97B, $10.98B and $13.28B (2025).

f2.evidence: GAAP operating margin rose from 4.4% in 2020 to 13.7% in 2025, but gross margin slipped from 78.2% to 77.5% and fell to 70.5% in Q2 2026 after the Armis deal.

f3.evidence: Equity is positive at $12.5 billion and operating cash flow was $5.4 billion in 2025, but debt rose to $7.5 billion at June 30, 2026, above cash and short-term investments of $4.7 billion.

f4.evidence: Operating income rose every year from $199 million (2020) to $1.82 billion (2025) and operating cash flow from $1.79 billion to $5.44 billion.

v1.evidence: It is the clear leader in IT service management (about 44% share), and buyers choose it because one platform connects IT, HR and customer requests, but in AI agents and CRM there is no consensus that it is best.

v2.evidence: ServiceNow is on Fortune's 100 Best Companies to Work For and Glassdoor's Best Places to Work in Tech and AI 2026.

c5.evidence: If it vanished, IT and HR departments at most Fortune 500 companies and many governments would be disrupted for months, but ordinary consumers would barely notice.
